meaningMnemonic: You see a cow in the evening. You get closer and realize it's doing a dance . All cows dance in the evening. Can you picture it? The cow is dancing, so majestic, in the setting sunlight.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means departure .

This radical is the sun with its hair sticking out. Why is the sun's hair sticking out like this? It ate wayyy too many sweet things causing it to have too much energy, making its hair stand on end. It also kind of looks like a sweet, sweet candy with the wrapper sticking out. Remember it how you'd like.

You say something and the flowers are right in agreement . The flowers see where you are coming from when you say what you say. You and the flowers are in complete agreement. Hints What did you say to the flowers that you are so in agreement about? Think about what you said.
readingMnemonic: You and the flowers are in agreement on the fact that neither of you like when a duck ( だく ) walks across the flowers. You don’t like having a duck walk on the flowers because the duck will poo in the flowers and then you have to worry about stepping in it. And the flowers just don’t like having duck poo in their face. Hints Imagine you are the flowers. There’s a duck. It’s making a poo. On you. Ew, man, that’s disgusting. Bleh.

meaningMnemonic: I’ll give you this bright plate if you agree to an alliance with me. I know you like things that are bright, and I know you like plates too. Therefore, this bright plate should be more than enough to convince you to enter into an alliance with me. Hints Look at this bright plate. Look at it. It’s awesome. It’s blinding. Hold it in your hands. Marvel at it. Wow. This plate is sweet.
readingMnemonic: The person you are trying to get in an alliance with you is the captain of the May flower ( めい ). You want to be in an alliance with the captain of the Mayflower because you really like boats. You want to ride on the Mayflower like, so bad. Hints This Mayflower boat is the best boat you ever did see. Hear the ocean around it as it bobs in the water, full sails billowing in the wind. Boats are cool.

meaningMnemonic: The commander radical and the commander kanji are the same! Hints Know your radicals, yo!
readingMnemonic: Who is the commander of Japan? The Shou gun ( しょう )! And if you ever say anyone else or vote for someone else or even THINK about someone else being the commander, he'll find you and cut off your head. Hints You better remember the Shougun is the commander of everything... or else...

meaningMnemonic: The nothing dance is still a dance ! Hints If you want to do the nothing dance, just clear your head so there's nothing in it, and then dance!
readingMnemonic: To help you do this dance you need some boo ze ( ぶ ). Just enough so it's easier to think of nothing, let all your fears go, and dance. Hints Feel the booze coursing through your veins as you dance like no one is watching.

meaningMnemonic: Your leader gets the blame if your company is in debt . They're the one who led you all into that debt, so they should get the blame too. Hints Picture the leader standing up in front of everyone as they blame him. He's holding a plaque with the amount of debt you're all in. Try to imagine what that number would be.
readingMnemonic: To pay off this debt your leader says you need to sell your cy borg ( さい ) to help the company. You fight him! You yell! You scream! The cyborg puts a half-human half-robot hand on your shoulder and shakes its head sadly. Hints Watch as your cyborg saves your company, even though it wasn't even his responsibility, from crippling debt. *sob* I can't believe your cyborg is gone!

meaningMnemonic: The leader of your branch became the leader from doing deed s. You can't rise to the rank of branch leader if you don't perform a certain number of deeds! Most of them good, I hope. Hints Picture the leader of your branch doing deeds around your office. Pulling out chairs for people sitting down, emptying the trash, balancing spreadsheets. All good deeds.
readingMnemonic: The deed he's currently working on is finding your lost key ( き ). He doesn't have to help, you're the one who lost your own house-combination-car key. But he's so used to doing deeds, he can't help but help. Hints Picture him doing this deed. He's crawling around on the floor looking for your key. You aren't really helping, you're just watching him do the deed of key-searching for you.

meaningMnemonic: A canopy and a helicopter are being compare d by a deer . The deer is standing very still (as deer do) and looking very slowly between the empty canopy and the helicopter sitting next to it. Hints Picture the deer comparing the two structures. It probably has no idea what they are, but it's trying very hard to understand what it's seeing anyway.
readingMnemonic: You walk forward, about to call out to the deer , when a ca r ( か ) suddenly appears out of no where and runs the deer over! Was this all just a trap set up to murder the deer?! Hints Deer get hit by cars all the time, but it was still really shocking . I mean it was right in front of you. The car could have hit you too!

meaningMnemonic: You count with your fingers in prison all of the mouth s and legs you've acquired. Soon you'll be able to make a big exchange with all of these body parts to get something awesome. Hints Imagine counting all of the mouths and legs you've pummeled off of the other prisoners. Exchange them for better loot!
readingMnemonic: You learned this type of exchange from the mighty Genghis Khan ( かん ). You read a book or watched a show about him once and you're pretty positive that Genghis Khan would exchange the body parts of his enemies all over the continents of Asia and Europe for nicer stuff. Hints Think back to when you were a kid and they would roll out those TVs on stands into the classrooms. Imagine watching a documentary on Genghis Khan's exchange routes where he bought and sold body parts. Educational!

meaningMnemonic: If there's a special woman in your life , she might eventually take your family name and make it her surname too. In Japan and other countries, tradition dictates that women change their last name when they get married and keep that name for the rest of their life. Their partner’s family name becomes their family name too. Hints Imagine having your surname changed for the rest of your life. How do you feel about having a different family name? Is it a big deal to you or does it not matter much?
readingMnemonic: Picture this special woman in your mind. She's changing her surname to yours and taking hold of your special sa ber ( せい ) as well. And it's... it's splitting in two! Hints Now you share a family name AND a holy blue saber! You can protect your legacy (and surname) hand in hand and saber in saber. (Or something like that.)

meaningMnemonic: The fang radical and the fang kanji are exactly the same! Fantastic. Oh, also it means tusk . It means fang and tusk. Hints Since the fang radical is the same as the fang kanji, that should be easy to remember. Tusks aren’t too different from fangs, so that shouldn’t be too hard to remember either.
readingMnemonic: Lots of animals have fang s, even ones that don't look like they do. The coolest fang-having animal is the ge cko ( げ )! They have pretty sharp little fangs in their mouths and they'll bite you if you keep tapping their glass cages like that. Cut it out. Hints Picture a gecko with cute little fangs. You can keep thinking they're cute as long as one never bites you. They may be little, but gecko fangs are no joke!

meaningMnemonic: There’s a stick next to the sun , reflecting on its former glory. The stick used to be a great tree, and the stick thinks that if it stays by the sun long enough it might return to its former form as a towering tree. Hints Pretend you are the stick. Really focus on your former self as you feel the sun warm you with its rays. Imagine yourself growing, larger and larger.
readingMnemonic: It's working, it's working! The stick is returning to its former state and... w-wuh? It sprouted a cu cumber ( きゅう ). Hints I guess this stick was formerly a cucumber tree. Or maybe it just tried so hard it pooped a cucumber. I don't care which one is true, you pick whatever you want to believe.

meaningMnemonic: Fire is one of a few things you'll need to fry things. Hints You need a few other things like a pan and some oil too, but fire is gonna be the most important for frying!
readingMnemonic: You love to fry things and are also an adventurous eater ( いた ). This means you'll fry and eat just about anything. Fried ostrich, fried alligator, fried chocolate, you name it! Hints Your being an adventurous eater of all things fried truly knows no bounds. What cursed combination of foods will you fry up tomorrow?!

meaningMnemonic: A boat will have at least one weapon , generally . Hints In general, you can assume a boat will have a weapon, but not all of them will.
readingMnemonic: Generally a boat with a weapon will be owned by Han ( はん ) Solo. Hints So of all the boats out there, generally all of them have weapons, and generally Han Solo will be on one.

meaningMnemonic: There’s a huge tsunami , caused by a giant brush , fast approaching you and your harbor . Hints This harbor is all you’ve got, it’s the backbone of your life. So how are you going to defend it from this tsunami caused by a giant brush?!
readingMnemonic: You’ll defend your harbor with your two ( つ ) best friends, that’s how! Luckily, your two friends specialize in defending harbors from giant brush-caused tsunamis. Quite the occupation. Hints “How are two of my friends going to stop an entire tsunami from destroying my dear harbor?”, you might ask yourself. Well don’t ask us, we don’t specialize in brush-caused tsunami harbor defence—we’re just a kanji learning website!

meaningMnemonic: If someone is sick feed them charcoal to heal them. Okay, so maybe you shouldn't feed it directly to them, but charcoal has amazing water filtration powers. So put charcoal in their water and the water will heal them right up. Hints Imagine being sick. Like sick as a dog sick. And then you take some charcoal, put it into your drinking water, and then you're healed!
readingMnemonic: You aren't the only one that needs to be heal ed, so you take your row ( りょう ) boat out onto the lake where your town gets its drinking water and you dump a bunch of charcoal into it! Now everyone will be healed when they drink. Hints Picture yourself rowing your row boat into the lake with huge chunks of solid charcoal. You carefully break them up and toss them over the side, so you can heal everyone.

meaningMnemonic: With a thread , a lion sews together all the rice he'll inherit from his parents one day. He's convinced his parents are going to try to keep some of his inheritance from him, so he's linking it all together so it can't go anywhere. Hints Picture this lion surrounded by the thousands of grains of rice he'll inherit from his parents. He's carefully threading them all together.
readingMnemonic: If you're going to inherit something from your parents, try to convince them to make it ca ke ( けい ), not rice. A single cake is much easier to keep track of and probably tastier (though it will be super stale by the time they die). Hints I'd much rather inherit a cake than a ton of hard to keep track of rice, like this poor lion.

meaningMnemonic: When you go on a scooter , anything valuable , you need to leave behind . Hints Rings, necklaces, wallets, phones? Don't take them on a scooter. Leave behind all that valuable stuff!
readingMnemonic: Anything you don't leave behind will be stolen by ea gles ( い ). Eagles like shiny, valuable things, especially ones that are bouncing around on you while you scoot by on a scooter. Hints If you keep too many of your valuables on you, the eagles might not leave you behind either! They'll just pick you up off the scooter and carry you and your valuables off to their nests!

meaningMnemonic: You tie a piece of thread to your turkey in order to maintain proximity to it. The turkey likes to run away, so you tie a thread to it. This way you can hold the other end and maintain your turkey. Hints Imagine holding onto a thread that is attached to a turkey. Feel the turkey tug against the thread as you struggle to maintain control.
readingMnemonic: The reason the turkey is tugging is because there’s an ea gle ( い ) swooping down to attack the turkey. You try to maintain control, but once you see the eagle as well, you let go of the thread. Hints Now you and the turkey and the eagle are all bumbling about in pandemonium. You try to maintain order but it’s not possible. What a kerfuffle.

meaningMnemonic: There is a big jackhammer in Nara . That jackhammer is the biggest in all the land and is on display in Nara, Japan. Hints Look at this big jackhammer. Look at it. It’s so big. Also it’s in Nara. Imagine being in Nara and looking at this big jackhammer. You’re all like, dang – that’s a big jackhammer.
readingMnemonic: What’s the first part of Nara ? Na ( な ). Well that’s easy. Hints Just keep in mind what the first part of Nara is. The first part of Nara is “na” so you’ll have no trouble remembering this one.

meaningMnemonic: You take a tree and slice it until you reach its nucleus . To get to the nucleus of the tree you have to make many a slice, but it’s possible. Hints Imagine slicing this tree smaller and smaller until you finally get to the nucleus of it. It’s super tiny so you have to view it in a microscope. What does it look like?
readingMnemonic: It looks like a cock ( かく ). And by cock I mean a male chicken – a rooster. Why does the nucleus of a tree look like a cock? Science is weird. Hints Look at this tree nucleus that looks like a cock. While you’re watching it, the nucleus goes “Cock-a-doodle-doo!”

meaningMnemonic: This canopy , after your departure , will become obsolete . The canopy was here to protect you, but no one will need it once you're gone. Hints During your departure you look back at the obsolete canopy just once. It's standing there, still and alone. It's a really sad sight.
readingMnemonic: When something becomes obsolete , you must write a hai ku ( はい ). Honestly, the best haiku are about something ending, so this is perfect. Hints My sweet canopy I don't need you anymore You are obsolete

meaningMnemonic: The South Dog gives you an offer . None of the other dogs in the North, East, or West offered you anything. Hints It is well known that dogs in the South are famous for their kindness and hospitality. It's customary to always offer something when a guest arrives.
readingMnemonic: The South Dog offer s you the services of Ken ( けん ) the samurai as you traverse his lands. Hints Ken offers to carry you, too. Imagine him offering this. You can choose whether or not to accept in your mind.

meaningMnemonic: There is a tsunami in the middle of the open sea . Luckily there are no ships around, so the tsunami in the middle of the open sea is not damaging to anyone. Hints Look at this tsunami in the middle of the open sea. When the tsunami isn’t destroying things and is just out there in the open sea it looks really majestic and pretty.
readingMnemonic: Someone dares you to go out to the open sea and surf on the middle of the tsunami. “ Oki ( おき ) doki,” you reply. You can’t refuse a dare. Every time someone dares you to do something, you always respond with “oki doki”. Hints You really regret saying oki doki this time. You don’t want to surf on a tsunami in the middle of the open sea. Imagine doing so. It’s terrifying and wet and you don’t even know how to surf. You’re going to die.

meaningMnemonic: Tsunami s get blame d because they pickle everything in their path. That means that everything smells of pickles after a tsunami. Hints Imagine a tsunami crashing over the land, being blamed by everyone. In its path are piles and piles of pickles, as far as the eye can see!
readingMnemonic: Looking at all those pickle s, you bend down and pick up two ( つ ) of them. One in each hand. You look at the pickles in your hand and wonder whether to try one. Hints Picture the two pickles and imagine what kind of pickles they are.

meaningMnemonic: Stick your fingers in your mohawk and pluck each hair out, one by one. Hints Imagine plucking the hairs out of your mohawk with your fingers. It's kind of hard to grab onto them at first, but eventually you're plucking them like it's nothing.
readingMnemonic: You want to pluck all your mohawk hair out because you're a techie ( てき ), and everyone at your techie job keeps making fun of you for your hair choices. "Techies should be bald!" your boss screamed. So here you are, plucking your hair out to fit in. Hints You didn't realize techies were so exclusive... but they just plucked and plucked at your self-esteem, until you decided to pluck your hair out of your own head.

meaningMnemonic: Escalator s are used to reach things. Hints Imagine yourself on an escalator. What is up above that you’re trying to reach?
readingMnemonic: You're riding the escalator trying to reach a delicious cu cumber ( きゅう ). Hints Cucumbers grow on trees sometimes, so you need to take escalators to get up there and reach them.

meaningMnemonic: A leader has clothes that he is quite reliant on. The leader needs his clothes to make him look like a leader. The leader has become more reliant on his clothes than he is on his actual skills as a leader! Hints Imagine this leader in his clothes. Look how reliant he is on them. Imagine what he would be without his clothes – nothing! And also, naked.
readingMnemonic: The leader has become so reliant on his clothes that his judgment has been clouded. His kingdom has become infested with ea gles ( い ) but the leader does nothing, trusting that his clothes will rout out the eagles if it is something that needs to be done. He’s become so reliant on his clothes that he’s started to become not so good a leader anymore. Hints Look at the leader as he shouts at his clothes he’s become so reliant on to do something. Hear the countless eagles screeching around as they terrorize the neighborhood. People scream and weep in the streets.

meaningMnemonic: Someone thread ed a turtle into long skinny pieces, making a rope . Hints A rope made of threaded turtles. Go ahead and grab onto it and see how it feels. A little rough, but strong.
readingMnemonic: The person making these threaded turtle rope s is none other than the local farmhand Joe ( じょう ). You watch him stretch and peel pieces of turtle off of turtles, then thread them together into a rope. Hints Besides being awful, where did Joe learn to thread turtles into ropes? Why does he have so many turtles despite living on such an inland farm? These are nice ropes that Joe is making though, and you kind of want to buy some.

meaningMnemonic: What kind of fish jumps from dirt to dirt ? A salmon ! Hints When you're at the river watching salmon jumping up stream, they keep jumping onto the dirt, flopping back into the water, then doing it again.
readingMnemonic: You make a drinking game out of watching the salmon going up stream. Every time one jumps onto the dirt, you drink a shot of 酒 ( さけ ). You realize you're drunk when you ask for more さけ but it comes out as しゃけ . Hints Salmon. Drink さけ . Salmon. Drink さけ . Salmon. Drink... "Ughhh.... I'm feeling tipsy... Hey, where's my しゃけ !?"

meaningMnemonic: You soak each foot in water before going out in the sun to take your first step . Stepping on the ground when it's been baking in the hot sun can burn your feet, so you're careful to make them wet with water before stepping outside even once. Hints Imagine each step on hot, sun-baked asphalt. The water under your feet sizzles, leaving steaming footprints where you stepped from.
readingMnemonic: Each step you take brings you closer to とう きょう . Unfortunately, the sun keeps getting hotter, meaning you have to take breaks between steps more often, to get your feet wet with even more water. But you're determined to reach とうきょう , no matter how many steps it takes. Hints Each step is taking you closer to とうきょう . Don't forget that, no matter how hard it seems, don't lose your motivation to keep stepping forward toward your goal. ♡

meaningMnemonic: A leader who's humble will stretch in front of everyone. They'll show that they have to get up every hour or so and stretch just like the rest of us. Hints The leader is humble and human, just like the rest of us, and has to stretch to stay healthy too. He's not some kind of god!
readingMnemonic: The leader is currently working hard to stretch in front of all of you, and as he does, he munches on some no ri ( の ) seaweed snacks. Then he starts stretching the nori too. Hints Watch as the leader stretches his body and the nori seaweed. He takes a bite, stretches the other way, then stretches out a piece for you to eat too. How humble of him!

meaningMnemonic: The sweet radical and the sweet kanji are exactly the same! Double sweet.
readingMnemonic: The sweet , sweet sensation is almost overwhelming. You gotta put on some sweet-resistant armor ( あま ) to protect you from all that sweetness. The armor will prevent you from having a sweet, sweet sweetness overload. Hints Put on the armor! Feel the sweetness begin to reflect off your armored body. Only a little gets through — just enough for the sweet flavor on your tongue to taste sweet, but not too sweet.

meaningMnemonic: You send your private sword man out with your shellfish so he can trade them. Shellfish were used as currency back in the olden days. And you aren't going to go out trading and dirty your own hands, no no. Trading your shellfish is the job for the private sword you hired! Hints Imagine your private sword holding a big bag of shellfish and going off to market to trade them.
readingMnemonic: While he's out making the trade for you, you decide to relax and do some bow ling ( ぼう ). In fact, you can't wait for the trade to be done because you're hoping he's going to come back with a new bowling ball for you. Hints Oh boy, I hope my private sword trades my shellfish for that new bowling ball I heard about!

meaningMnemonic: A bundle of geoduck s is something you can always trust . Hints A bundle of geoducks will never lie, never let you down, and never disappoint you. You can trust them completely.
readingMnemonic: While you can trust a bundle of geoducks, never ever trust rye ( らい ) bread. Hints Imagine a bundle of geoducks and a piece rye bread. Think about how you can trust the geoducks but you can't trust the rye bread.

meaningMnemonic: You run and call out to people at the same time because you're super ultra excited right now. You have a super crazy amount of energy you need to get out with your running and calling. Hints You're going for an ultra run, calling out with your super loud voice right down the middle of the street.
readingMnemonic: You're just becoming ultra tired when you hear a terrifying sound. It's Mrs. Chou ( ちょう ) barreling down toward you. "WERE YOU CALLING FOR ME, CHILD?!" she screams. Hints Mrs. Chou is super ultra scary. And if you don't kick it into super ultra high gear she's going to catch up to you and make you super ultra dead.

meaningMnemonic: There were lots of things that were above you when you were small that you would need a stool to reach, so you just asked your aunt or uncle to get them for you. Hints Your parents didn't want you having those things, which is why they put them up high, but your aunt and uncle would always spoil you and get them for you.
readingMnemonic: You ask your aunt and uncle to help you reach your special o bi ( お ) from high up in the closet. Hints You aren't supposed to wear your obi unless it's a special occasion, but your aunt and uncle don't know that. Now you can run around with it on your head and your parents can't stop you by putting it up high!

meaningMnemonic: When you see a tsunami coming, courage will well up inside you, giving you the power to save everyone before you get washed away! Hints Really feel the courage welling up inside of you in the face of this terrifying tsunami. Connect it to some physical feeling—perhaps you can feel it welling up in your chest.
readingMnemonic: Whom does that courage well up inside of? You ( ゆう )! In fact, YOU feel like there is a never ending well of courage bursting out of you now. You are going to be a hero! Hints Who wells up with courage? You do!

meaningMnemonic: You want to put this towel over this scarecrow , but you have to measure its width first. If the towel doesn't have a greater width than the scarecrow, some of it will be showing. Which you definitely don't want. Hints The scarecrow creeps you out. You don't want to look at it anymore, so you're standing eerily close to it measuring its width, so you can hide it forever.
readingMnemonic: You finish measuring the width of the scarecrow and the width of the towel, and you realize you're the width of a haba nero ( はば ) pepper short. This is fine, you grow those. This is a whole field of habaneros! So you pluck one off the nearest plant, tape it to the cloth, and cover that scarecrow right up. Hints Do you know the width of a habanero? It's one scarecrow minus one cloth.

meaningMnemonic: It is obsolete so we must stop it. No more of it anymore. This is abolition .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: 死刑制度廃止には、賛成ですか、反対ですか。
sentences.english: Do you agree or disagree with the abolition of the death penalty?

meaningMnemonic: I will accept and I have agreement in the matter. I have come to acceptance .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: コウイチはアメリカ合衆国の大統領になることを渋々受諾した。
sentences.english: Koichi reluctantly agreed to become the president of the United States.

meaningMnemonic: We are of the same alliance . We are in an alliance .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: ああ、そういうことか。トーフグは一番のライバル会社と同盟を組んだんだよ。
sentences.english: Oh, now I see what happened. Tofugu formed an alliance with its closest competitor.

meaningMnemonic: An aunt feels like a mother sometimes, but she's still an aunt after all.
readingMnemonic: The reading for the 母 part is just the first は in はは , rendaku'd. You can also think of your aunt as a sheep, too, if you'd like. Baaaah!

sentences.japanese: 叔母は学校の先生をしています。
sentences.english: My aunt is a school teacher.

meaningMnemonic: A bad example is a bad example and is something you don't want. This is a formal expression and less common than 悪い例 (bad example) or 良くない例 (not good example).
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 悪例をのこす
sentences.english: to leave behind a bad example

sentences.japanese: 悪例をあげる
sentences.english: to give a bad example

sentences.japanese: 悪例を作る
sentences.english: to set a bad example

sentences.japanese: 日本語を学ぶ時には、いい例だけでなく、悪例を学ぶことも必要です。
sentences.english: When learning Japanese, it is necessary to learn from good examples as well as bad examples.

sentences.japanese: コウイチは悪例のかたまりだ。
sentences.english: Koichi is a cluster of bad examples.

sentences.japanese: 僕の両親は、今後の寝る時間に悪例を残すことになるからって、絶対に夜更かしさせてくれないんだ。
sentences.english: My parents never let me stay up late because they believed it would set a bad precedent for future bedtimes.

meaningMnemonic: I would like to offer my blood to someone else in the form of a blood donation .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: 車が移動献血車に衝突するのを見ました。
sentences.english: I saw a car bump into the mobile blood bank van.

meaningMnemonic: A debt ticket is a bond . You buy it from the government and then they pay it back to you with interest... in theory.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: 債券市場は何時まで開いてますか。
sentences.english: What time is the bond market open until?

sentences.japanese: 東京都は来たるオリンピックのため、追加で債券を発行した。
sentences.english: The Tokyo Metropolitan Government has issued additional bonds for the upcoming Olympics.

sentences.japanese: 債券取引は、一億円単位で売買できない人には不利なレートになってるんですよ。
sentences.english: Current bond rates are no good for people who can't trade them in one hundred million yen increments.

meaningMnemonic: This very common food is parent and child rice bowl , aka a parent and child rice bowl . The parent is a chicken. The child is an egg. This can also be called chicken and egg rice bowl , or simply oyako-don .
readingMnemonic: This is 親子 ( おやこ ) plus 丼 , and all three kanji use their kun'yomi readings. The full name is おやこどんぶり , but people usually say おやこどん for short. You learned the full どんぶり reading with the vocab word 丼 , but here's a refresher: When you want to make a chicken and egg rice bowl , you have to ask Don Brie ( どんぶり ) for the rice bowl. He's the mafia boss who hoards all the rice bowls to eat his cheese out of — remember him? Don't get on Don Brie's bad side, or no oyako-don for you!

sentences.japanese: 親子丼ほど美味しいものはない。
sentences.english: There's nothing more delicious than a chicken and egg rice bowl.

sentences.japanese: 個人的には親子丼よりも他人丼の方が好きなんです。
sentences.english: Personally, I like tanin-don more than oyako-don.

sentences.japanese: あの親子丼超まずかったよね！トイレで吐いちゃったよ！

meaningMnemonic: A same window meeting is a meeting with people who spent a long time gazing out of the same classroom window as you. Who are those people? meaningMnemonic: This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. This adjective describes things that are valuable in a way that transcends monetary worth, so it means noble or invaluable . While 尊い is used for things you honor from the heart, 貴い leans toward a dignified, noble kind of value — the kind tied to high status or social rank. Because of that, you may encounter 貴い in stories about historical class systems or old social hierarchies. It doesn't appear as commonly as 尊い in modern Japanese, but you may still see it in descriptions of someone's noble presence or the sense of dignity they give off.

In case you forgot, here's a mnemonic to help you: How can you tell if someone comes from a noble background? Just check their toe toe ( とうと ). Most noble families are pretty inbred, so a lot of their members will have a big toe (the long とう ) with another small toe growing out of it (short と ). This is a common birth defect among inbred aristocrats. Of course, from their point of view, it's invaluable proof of how noble and superior they are.
